articles.title_zh: China opposes arms race in space, official document shows
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, Oct 23 (Reuters) – China on Friday released a document detailing its official position on “space governance” that reaffirms its opposition to the weaponisation of outer space and to a space arms race.
• China opposes the weaponisation and militarisation of outer space and is against its use “for activities that harm other countries’ sovereignty, security, or development interests,” according to the document, which was released by its foreign ministry
• China opposes offensive military policies in outer space and calls for “every possible effort to prevent an arms race in outer space”, it says
• The document adds that “the risk of an arms race in outer space and the trend toward turning it into a battlefield have become the greatest threats and challenges to space security”
• The document calls for regulating commercial space activities and says China encourages “the development of the space economy”. It says commercial space activities should “not infringe upon the lawful rights and interests of other countries, and in particular avoid unlawfully intervening in other countries’ armed conflicts and internal affairs”
• The document also calls for outer space to be explored and used for peaceful purposes. It says all countries’ right to access, explore and use space should be safeguarded
(Reporting by Xiuhao Chen, Yukun Zhang and Liz Lee; Editing by Emelia Sithole-Matarise, Aidan Lewis)

Brent crude increase follows Tehran threatening retaliatory attacks on Gulf refineries and datacentres
Business live – latest updates
Oil has hit its highest level in more than five months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by 1% on Friday morning to above $115 a barrel – its highest level since May.
The increase came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran .
Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”
Oil had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia , which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”

Rescuers race to mountainous Baqing county where 300 homes have collapsed in the 7.0-magnitude quake that struck on Thursday night
All efforts need to be focused on search and rescue for survivors and treating the injured, President Xi Jinping instructed on Friday morning, after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake killed 16 and injured 65 in China’s Tibet autonomous region overnight.
“The disaster-hit area is located in a high-altitude region with cold weather. It is imperative to closely monitor seismic activity and weather changes and implement rescue operations accordingly, while preventing secondary disasters,” he said, according to state news agency Xinhua.
Xi added that emergency rescue supplies needed to be allocated and those affected in the disaster should be settled properly, while damaged infrastructure should be repaired as soon as possible.
The weather in the region is minus 5 degrees Celsius (23 Fahrenheit), with a small chance of snow.

articles.title_orig: Health officials race to trace source of Nigeria's Ebola infection
articles.title_zh: Health officials race to trace source of Nigeria's Ebola infection
articles.content_orig:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda
Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.
The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda , Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.
The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.
The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.
Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.
Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.
Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”
The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.
Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.
Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.
The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.
The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

China’s domestic online beauty sales are falling as C-beauty companies are ramping up export efforts and moving into international retail channels. The gap suggests a deliberate pivot from C-beauty toward overseas growth, targeting the categories and regions that K-beauty has spent the past decade winning over.
According to Jefferies’ China online beauty tracker , the country recorded a 6% year-on-year cosmetics sales decline in September 2026. Skin care fell 6.1%, while color cosmetics went down 5.2%.
However, at the same time, data from the Korea International Trade Association (KITA) shows China climbing from seventh place to fifth in global cosmetics exports. The trade body says China’s color cosmetics exports amount to nearly three times that of Korea’s.
C-beauty company Proya, meanwhile, has opened a European Innovation Center Laboratory in France and has announced it will begin selling across 400 Ulta Beauty stores in the US next month.
“This Europe Innovation Center Laboratory connects the European and Chinese ecosystems to draw on combined strengths and create new innovation capabilities,” says Hou Juncheng, founder and chairman of Proya Cosmetics.
The center is not the first bridge between Chinese and European beauty. French ingredient suppliers have been actively pursuing partnerships with Chinese cosmetics brands, and many Chinese perfumers train in France. The country’s Cosmetic Valley, meanwhile, has set up a Shanghai-based fragrance and cosmetics embassy to encourage collaboration between the two markets . Chinese beauty brands are expanding overseas, targeting markets where K-beauty has established a strong presence.
With color cosmetics exports already outpacing Korea’s and a growing foothold in US and European retail, C-beauty appears to be borrowing the playbook that got K-beauty onto global shelves.
The September figures from Jefferies’ tracker show many multinational beauty giants experiencing declining figures in China. L’Oréal fell 5%, Estée Lauder 8%, Procter & Gamble 20%, Shiseido 24%, and LVMH 26%.
Beiersdorf and Galderma were the only multinationals to grow, supported by their Nivea and Cetaphil brands. At the brand level, dermatological skin care like CeraVe and Cetaphil grew (35% and 58%, respectively), while Bobbi Brown fell 31%. Among domestic players, Mao Geping grew 26%, and Proya grew 1%.
As demand becomes increasingly selective, and derma-brands gain ground, Jefferies’ findings show skin care and color cosmetics accounting for over 80% of China’s beauty market. Both categories initially gave rise to K-beauty.
According to KITA, China’s cosmetic exports reached ₩8.14 trillion (US$6.1 billion) from January to July 2026, up 24% from ₩6.55 trillion (US$4.9 billion) a year earlier. The figures lifted China to fifth in global export rankings, behind France in the lead and South Korea in second place.
In color cosmetics, China has already overtaken Korea. Exports of lip and eye makeup, powders, and nail products totaled ₩1.88 trillion (US$1.41 billion) from January to July, about 2.9 times Korea’s ₩644.7 billion (US$484 million).
From January to July 2026, China’s lip makeup exports were 1.7 times Korea’s, and its eye makeup exports were 3.5 times. China’s exports grew 17% to 33% across all four color cosmetics categories (lip, eye, powders, and nail products), while Korea’s lip makeup and nail product exports fell 15% and 15.6%, respectively. Proya is expanding its international presence with a new research laboratory in France.
According to The Asia Business Daily, Kecia Steelman, CEO of Ulta Beauty, raised C-beauty during the company’s 2026 Q2 fiscal earnings call. She is quoted as saying, “[We are launching] Proya, the number one skin care brand in China. So it’s not just about K-Beauty anymore.”
Proya’s US launch will be the first time a Chinese premium skin care brand joins Ulta’s online and physical networks at the same time. The rollout is planned for November this year, and with it, Proya says it is “moving beyond mere product export to brand globalization.”
To expand, the company says, “brands must not only enter overseas markets but also earn a permanent place in consumers’ daily skin care regimens and secure a voice within elite global beauty narratives.”
Securing that voice, Proya has inaugurated its Europe Innovation Center Laboratory in France, with a 450 square meter site containing 76 pieces of equipment and seven dedicated researchers. The lab will focus on research and innovation in skin longevity, biology, biotechnology, and sustainable ingredients.
The lab will collaborate with the Hangzhou Longwu center in China, which handles formulation, ingredients, safety, and efficacy, and the Shanghai center, which works on hair care and the scalp microbiome.
Proya’s international push comes after its namesake brand, which accounts for around 70% of group revenue, posted a 7% sales decline in H1 2026. The drop was the company’s first after years of uninterrupted growth since its 2017 Shanghai listing. Jefferies says the brand returned to 1% growth in September, but the overseas expansion appears partly aimed at offsetting soft momentum.

articles.title_orig: French authorities deploy 70,000 officers for Saturday protests; Louvre and other museums closed
articles.title_zh: French authorities deploy 70,000 officers for Saturday protests; Louvre and other museums closed
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — Some 70,000 law enforcement officers will be deployed across France on Saturday while the Louvre and several other major Paris museums will be closed as authorities seek to prevent renewed violence during planned protests.
Protests last week devolved into mayhem , with people setting fires, storming public buildings, smashing shop windows, looting and clashing with police. It was France’s most violent unrest in years.
Demonstrators plan to take to the streets again Saturday to denounce the high cost of living. Students, members of the CGT labor union and activists from the “ yellow vest ” movement, whose demonstrations against social injustice shook France in 2018 and 2019, are all set to join.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said some 70,000 police officers and gendarmes would be deployed, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons. In addition, elite police units will help secure public buildings like city halls in a “highly mobile” security operation, he said.
“There have been numerous calls from radical far-left groups on social media to commit acts of violence and vandalism. There have also been renewed calls for looting, with those messages clearly being spread by rioters,” Nuñez said at a news conference.
“We will be absolutely uncompromising” with those involved in violence, he added, warning that police will have a “very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences.”
In a statement to The Associated Press, the Culture Ministry said the Louvre, the Orsay and Picasso museums as well as the Grand Palais would be closed. The ministry called on all institutions under its authority to adopt any necessary measures to ensure “visitor safety, staff protection and the preservation of artworks,” according to the statement.
After two days when admission was by invitation only, Art Basel Paris opened to the public Friday — but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program. One of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, Art Basel includes exhibitions by 211 international galleries at Paris’ Grand Palais.
“This decision has not been taken lightly, and the safety of everyone involved in the fair remains our utmost priority,” organizers said in a statement Thursday.
Saloni Doshi, an art collector who traveled to Paris from India for the fair, grew worried last Saturday as she saw the fires and panicked people, and she received phone calls from friends asking whether Paris was safe. She agreed with the organizers’ rationale to close.
Antoine Donzeaud and Elisa Rigoulet, the owners of the gallery exo exo, felt the same.
“We understand this decision, which we consider reasonable and consistent with the urgency of the social demands currently unfolding in France,” they said in a text message.
A demonstration Saturday in the city of Orléans, about 70 miles south of Paris, will also be closely watched.
About 50 organizations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organizers include labor unions, left-wing political parties, student organizations and anti-racism groups.
Hugues Moutouh, the prefect of the Loiret region, said that 20,000 to 30,000 demonstrators from across the country were expected.
Le Pen, whom opinion polls place as the front-runner in next year’s election, accused left-wing organizations and political parties of trying to “disrupt a political party’s democratic congress,” on news broadcaster Franceinfo.
Still, she said she had “no concerns” about security because the government had “recognized the need for measures allowing the congress to proceed safely.”

articles.title_orig: People are fixing their TV OSes with Claude
articles.title_zh: People are fixing their TV OSes with Claude
articles.content_orig:
Users are getting fed up with the barrage of ads and data tracking on TVs and are looking to AI vibe coding for the answer.
Users are getting fed up with the barrage of ads and data tracking on TVs and are looking to AI vibe coding for the answer.
Vibe coding has reached TVs. Social media is awash with posts from people using LLMs and open-source tools to remove ads and tracking, trim bloat so the OS runs faster, and even completely change the look and organization of their homescreens. While a lot of it is fun — one user turned their TV homescreen into a Pokémon town — I think there’s a level of frustration behind it, too. And TV companies should take notice.
Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox , and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things — remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you’re watching — without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV’s built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokémon one below.
Most of the projects we’ve seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don’t require root access or firmware hacking, and they’re reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android’s ability to install custom launchers — in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too.
As Verge friend Chris Person notes in his Aftermath post , none of this requires AI. These projects take advantage of capabilities that already exist in Android, and in some cases reinvent the wheel. Android debloating programs that use ADB have been around for years, and so have replacement launchers that make Google TV OS look like Apple TV . AI just made the process easier and faster.
There’s nothing similar available for Samsung’s Tizen OS or LG’s webOS, apart from rooting the TV, which is a whole different level of hacking and device control. While there’s a webOS vibe hack for LG TVs that’s based on cleanyourtv, it doesn’t really do the same thing, essentially streaming the Apple TV-like launcher from an always-on device on the same network. They also won’t work for Roku or Vizio’s SmartCast.
These projects, or any OS vibe coding someone might attempt, won’t necessarily stop all data collection. A good basic rule is that if the TV is connected to the internet, it’s collected at least some data. Dumbtv blocks certain manufacturer and ad partner addresses your TV sends data to, but since it’s usually encrypted during transit, knowing what exactly gets sent is impossible. The data blocking is similar to what you can do with Pi-hole to block malicious DNS requests on your network.
TVs have increasingly become a means for companies to gather viewing data and serve up ads. By using automatic content recognition (ACR) and digital fingerprinting, manufacturers are able to know what content you’re watching, send that information to their ad partners, and then display targeted ads on the TV.
ACR isn’t just used for ads, though. It allows companies to measure audience metrics, and it can feed show recommendations based on what you’ve watched. It’s important to note that users need to agree to ACR tracking, and there are ways to opt out of it after the fact in a TV’s menus (although those options are not always easy to find). There are also options in most menus — again, usually buried — for turning off targeted ads.
But even after doing that, there’s always concern that companies still collect some amount of your data and use it in ways you might not be comfortable with. Whether or not it’s true does little to assuage those fears. The weekend of vibe coding, on the other hand, is a way for people to try and take control of their TVs to get the user experience they want.
There are also dangers to vibe-coding your TV. One person who tried to vibe-hack a Samsung TV with Claude bricked it. The only way to fully avoid ACR, ads, or any type of data collection is to never connect it to the internet. A firmware download to a USB stick can apply critical updates instead of Wi-Fi or Ethernet. If you still want to stream content, a streaming device that doesn’t use ACR , like an Apple TV 4K (grab a last-generation model before the expensive new one replaces it), is an option. But any streaming requires sharing some amount of your data with someone to function properly.
The biggest takeaway from the vibe-coding weekend is that the current state of TV OSes has people fed up. Most people aren’t going to stop watching TV anytime soon, but the experience needs to improve. The ads, the data collection, and the cluttered layouts are too aggravating. AI now allows anyone to code their own solution, and it’s only going to get easier. If TV manufacturers don’t take note and make changes, there’s a chance that users will make the changes for them.

articles.title_orig: Amex to Slash 5% of Headcount as CEO Seeks to Reduce Expenses
articles.title_zh: Amex to Slash 5% of Headcount as CEO Seeks to Reduce Expenses
articles.content_orig:
American Express is cutting thousands of employees as the leading credit card company prepares for artificial intelligence to take over more of its internal processes.
Amex is eliminating 5% of its global workforce and taking a $336 million restructuring charge, CEO Stephen Squeri told analysts Friday on the company's third-quarter earnings call. The firm had almost 77,000 employees at the end of 2025.
CFO Christophe Le Caillec told CNBC in an interview that the restructuring charge was to make American Express "leaner, more agile, and also to prepare for AI."
"You don't want to automate processes that are not optimally structured," Le Caillec said. "So what we're doing here is to reduce layers and increase spans of controls, so that we can automate and take advantage of AI in the coming quarters and the coming years."
The Amex announcement reflects a broader trend across financial services, where banks are working to replace repetitive roles with AI automation. On Thursday, Barclays confirmed plans to trim 5,000 jobs — also roughly 5% of its staff — in another tech-driven cost initiative. The moves come even as the sector is enjoying robust profits from growing consumer spending and resilient credit.
During the analyst call, Squeri said that the charge was to improve the company's efficiency.
"We've got good momentum, but to accelerate innovation and win over the next few years, we needed to become [a] more agile and efficient organization," Squeri said.
"We believe this exercise will help us operate and execute more effectively and give us greater capacity to invest in our business priorities," he said.

articles.title_orig: SK Hynix Stock Jumps After Scrapping U.S. IPO of Memory-Chip Unit
articles.title_zh: SK Hynix Stock Jumps After Scrapping U.S. IPO of Memory-Chip Unit
articles.content_orig:
Shares of South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix closed higher on Friday, reversing losses of as much as 3% earlier in the session after the company's decision to halt a review of a potential U.S. initial public offering for its subsidiary Solidigm.
The stock reversed earlier losses to close 4.4% higher.
Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for APAC at investment platform eToro, said the stock's rebound suggested that concerns over a potential Solidigm IPO had been weighing on investor sentiment.
"SK Hynix shareholders have got the outcome they were pushing for," Gilbert said, adding that "in the short term, it removes a governance worry and keeps Solidigm's value inside the company."
He explained that SK Hynix faces the challenge of funding Solidigm's growth without compromising share buybacks and dividends, as the company needs to demonstrate a credible funding plan as it prepares to report earnings next week.
"Solidigm will halt its review of potential pre-IPO and IPO options," the company said in the statement after assessing recent capital market conditions and share price trends, while also exploring various funding options to finance a new U.S. semiconductor fabrication plant amid growing demand for AI memory.
The chip manufacturer said an IPO could have helped fund Solidigm's expansion while providing greater financial flexibility for shareholder returns, including dividends, share buybacks and share cancellations.
However, financial market volatility had increased and contributed to a broader correction in semiconductor stocks, prompting SK Hynix to reassess whether an IPO would benefit existing shareholders.
SK Hynix said that Solidigm's existing production facilities had limited capacity to meet rising AI-driven memory demand, underscoring the need for additional manufacturing capacity in the U.S.
The decision also follows regulatory scrutiny in South Korea.
The country's financial regulator said Monday that a potential U.S. listing of Solidigm could violate South Korean rules restricting dual listings, according to Reuters.
Financial Supervisory Service Governor Lee Chan-jin said regulators were examining whether the IPO would require a review under the country's rules designed to protect minority shareholders.
SK Hynix said Solidigm's investment needs remain unchanged and that it would continue exploring alternative financing options to support the subsidiary's growth and enhance shareholder value.

articles.title_orig: ASUS ProArt P16 Review: A Sleek Showcase For NVIDIA's RTX Spark
articles.title_zh: ASUS ProArt P16 Review: A Sleek Showcase For NVIDIA's RTX Spark
articles.content_orig:
But it's really only meant for AI fanatics.
ASUS's first laptop featuring an RTX Spark chip confirms what I originally thought: NVIDIA's new PC platform really isn't meant for everyone. The ProArt P16 is yet another one of the company's premium notebooks focused on power-hungry creators — except this time, it's running NVIDIA's first major PC chipset, instead of an Intel or AMD processor. Outside of the hype from Microsoft and NVIDIA, who are positioning RTX spark as a complete "reinvention" of the PC, the ProArt P16 is simply a nice laptop. It's particularly appealing if you're running local AI models, since it can squeeze up to 128GB of RAM into a relatively slim case.
The downsides? It's incredibly expensive, with a starting price of $2,800 and staggering increases as you add more RAM. (Spoiler: Our review model costs $7,000, mostly thanks to its 128GB of RAM.) And even though the ASUS P16 can play games well, you're paying far more here than you would for a dedicated gaming laptop.
Much like the ProArt PX13 we reviewed earlier this year, the ProArt P16 shows just how far ASUS has come with premium laptops. It sports a beautiful and sturdy aluminum case, a wonderfully bright 16-inch OLED screen, a luxuriously-spaced keyboard and a similarly enormous haptic touchpad. It's MacBook-esque in its sleekness, except it has an ASUS badge. The ProArt P16 is even lighter than the 16-inch MacBook Pro, clocking in at 3.9 pounds, compared to Apple's 4.7 pounds.
From afar, the ASUS P16 doesn't look particularly special. But peek under the hood, and you'll quickly see what makes it different. It's powered entirely by NVIDIA's RTX Spark system-on-a-chip, which brings together a 20-core Arm CPU, a modern Blackwell GPU, and, as I mentioned, up to 128GB of unified memory. If that sounds familiar, it's because it's very similar to the way Apple has configured its M-series chips, which was the main reason we've adored that company's computers since 2020.
Unlike Apple's chip revamp, RTX Spark won't completely replace x86 hardware from Intel and AMD. You can think of it as a new fork of PC design aimed squarely at AI researchers and enthusiasts. RTX Spark is also meant to coexist with Qualcomm's Snapdragon X chips, which use a similar Arm-based design for entry-level and midrange systems.
As I've previously reported , there's a good chance that, despite a niche audience, RTX Spark will likely be a win for Windows PCs in general. Competition is always good for consumers — with NVIDIA planting its flag in the Windows world, you can certainly bet that AMD, Intel and Qualcomm will up their game with future hardware. Unfortunately, RTX Spark likely won't help PCs revert back to their pre-AI boom pricing. It's yet another memory-hungry platform at a time when AI has already driven RAM prices through the roof.
At least NVIDIA and PC makers are trying to stuff in all of the pro-level features RTX Spark owners may want. In addition to the hardware I've mentioned above, the ASUS P16 also squeezes in just about every port you'd need, including three USB-C connections, USB Type A, HDMI, a headphone jack and a full-sized SD card reader. Ethernet would be nice, but that's become a true rarity in thinner, pro-grade laptops.
Using the ASUS P16 with RTX Spark reminded me of the first time I turned on a MacBook Pro with an M-series chip: Everything about it feels lightning fast. I was up and running in no time, and I felt unstoppable as I downloaded several massive files simultaneously to start my benchmarking process. But of course, for a $7,000 system with 128GB of RAM, it damn well better feel speedy.
I'll admit, I was a bit surprised by the ASUS P16's initial benchmark scores: Its PCMark 10 (Applications) figure was 3,000 points lower than the ultra-slim ASUS A16 I tested earlier this year, which was powered by a Snapdragon X2 Elite chip. The RTX Spark system also lagged behind slightly in Geekbench 6's single-threaded CPU test, which is a sign that Qualcomm's chips just have more capable CPUs.
But really, the star of the RTX Spark's design is its GPU, NPU and unified memory, and those all stood out in other tests. The ASUS P16 RTX Spark was 4,700 points higher than the MacBook Pro with M5 Max in Geekbench 6's GPU benchmark, which tests overall graphics performance. The ProArt P16 also scored 3,895 points in UL Procyon's AI Computer Vision 2 benchmark, compared to 3,267 points from that same MacBook. Its 1,519 score in Procyon's AI Image Generation test was also 600 points higher than Apple's. Those Procyon benchmarks all clearly benefitted from the RTX Spark chip' s beefy graphics power.
Beyond benchmarks, the ASUS P16 was able to run OpenClaw and the large Qwen3.8 27B model, which alone takes up 42GB of RAM, while still leaving me with a ton of RAM for other tasks. At the same time, I was even able to play Control: Resonant and Cyberpunk 2077 at high quality settings without breaking a sweat. Sure, the fans sounded like they were about to lift the P16 off my desk, but there was never any noticeable slowdown in performance.
NVIDIA has previously said that the RTX Spark's graphics hardware is about on-par with the RTX 5070 mobile GPU, while also drawing much less power, and that held true in my testing. I was able to play Control Resonant at 70 fps while rendering the game in 1,440p with "ultra" graphics settings, ray-tracing set to medium and 4x frame generation. That's a game where the overall fidelity matters more than a triple-digit framerate, but I could get the ProArt P16 to 120 fps by lowering the graphics settings.
While I didn't have much trouble running other games, including Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Gears of War: E-Day , there's a chance you'll have trouble with some titles. Since RTX Spark is based on an Arm CPU, it has to rely on Microsoft's Prism emulator to handle most games. That introduces an immediate performance drop, as well as potential issues. There are native Arm64 builds for popular titles like Fortnite , DOTA 2, Marvel Rivals and the upcoming World of Warcraft: Forever , so there's a chance that compatibility concerns will melt away in a few years. But if you don't want to worry about emulation troubles at all, you're better off with a standard gaming laptop running an Intel or AMD chip.
There are also similar compatibility concerns for older Windows software in general, though I didn't encounter any weirdness during my testing. The whole Windows on Arm experience received a huge upgrade when Copilot+ systems launched two years ago, and since then, it seems like Microsoft has worked to make its x86 emulation even more seamless.
The ProArt P16's 16-inch "Lumina Pro" OLED screen was perfect for Control Resonant : It was able to show off dark black levels and extreme contrast in darker environments, but it also seared my eyeballs at times with its peak 1,600-nit luminance. It's definitely one of the brightest OLED screens I've seen on a laptop, and it directly competes with Apple's Mini LED MacBook Pro displays, which also top out at 1,600 nits. That extreme brightness also made the ProArt P16 perfect for getting work done outside in the sun, as I try to eke out every bit of warmth I can before winter arrives.
I was similarly impressed by every other aspect of the ASUS ProArt P16. Its wide keyboard and luscious key depth made typing a dream, and it also has one of the best haptic touchpads I've ever seen on a Windows PC. While it would have been nice to have a quad-speaker setup, which has become increasingly common in large premium laptops, the ProArt P16's dual speakers still sounded solid. They also offer a bit of spatial audio support, thanks to Dolby Atmos.
The only major downside to the ProArt P16, like most jet-black PCs, is that it's a horrendous fingerprint magnet. Marks start appearing the instant you touch it, and heaven forbid you eat anything oily while using it. It takes just a few minutes for the P16 to start looking like a gross mess, and

articles.title_orig: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.title_zh: The young Americans choosing Y2K cars over shiny new SUVs: ‘I get so much crap from people’
articles.content_orig:
People under 35 are hunting for no-frills rides they can pay for in cash and fix themselves – defying expectations to take on steep loans
J ack Price joined the Marines in fall 2021 knowing he would need a car to get around base and that he couldn’t afford a new one. A joyless, month-long search through dealer classifieds and Facebook Marketplace listings ended when his mother spotted a 2010 Volkswagen Jetta posted on her office listserv by a co-worker moving abroad. With just 60,000 miles (96,560km) on themeter, the car (a manual!) was mechanically sound, and the air conditioning, sunroof and Bluetooth radio worked too. At $6,000, it was a steal. Price paid in cash.
Five years on, the Jetta, which he called the Pewter Pebble, is still carting him from A to B in unassuming style. “I’ve completely driven it into the ground,” says the 30-year-old, who lives in Los Angeles. “All over bases, cross-country a couple times, not really lovingly. I get so much crap from people, but not people my age.”
For generations, buying a first new car has been a rite of passage in the US, the clearest sign of a young person responsibly striking out on their own. But younger millennials and gen Z are increasingly finding that path blocked. The average new vehicle costs more than $50,000, an alarming figure that reflects Americans’ insatiable appetite for progressively larger SUVs and pickups. Meanwhile, adults under 35 are disappearing from showroom floors, accounting for less than 10% of new vehicle registrations in 2024 – a new low.
According to the credit reporting agency Experian, the average monthly car payment in the US is $765 for a new car and $542 for a used one, with the loan terms now stretching to six, even seven, years. A record 21% of new-car buyers pay $1,000 or more a month , according to the autos research group Edmunds. And that’s before factoring in maintenance, fluctuating gas prices and the eye-watering insurance premiums often charged to drivers under 35.
For many young Americans already under the strain of student loans, high housing costs and an unforgiving labor market, buying a new car or even a newer used one is out of the question. Enter the Y2K car – the retro ride that has become a trendy romantic choice for some younger Americans. “There’s definitely a golden era of cars from the late 90s and early 2000s that people just really want all of a sudden,” says Charlie Spears, a service adviser at an independently owned repair shop in Atlanta who conducts prepurchase inspections of used cars on demand. “A lot of people just want something that’s not going to fail them.”
Y2K cars don’t encompass everything produced in that era. They are the ones that simply won’t die. Think wedge-shaped Honda Accords and slab-sided Toyota Camrys: dependable, hand-me-down transport that can last 150,000 miles or more with routine maintenance. (Price’s Jetta, which was built at the end of a model production run that began in 2005, just makes the cut.) They’re economical to run and relatively inexpensive to insure, owing to their drastically lower worth. Best of all, the purchase price is low enough to pay in cash. Even when buyers need a loan – at steep interest rates as modern cars have in effect become mortgage payments on wheels – they can pay it off in a fraction of the time it takes to finance a newer car.
The supply of these bargains is dwindling: used vehicles priced under $15,000, the sweet spot for Y2K cars, have shrunk from 21% of inventory a year ago to 15% , according to industry analysis from Cox Automotive – numbers that speak to the demand for affordable cars. “Part of the draw is the nostalgia factor – people wanting cars they grew up with,” says Consumer Reports’ autos expert Keith Barry. “An old car with the right music on is kind of the closest thing to a time machine.”
On social media, the Y2K car has emerged as an ironic status symbol – a marker of maturity, grit and lack of pretense. Defects – busted aircon, glitchy windows, bits and bobs that have failed, fallen off or been held on with gaffer tape – are simply treated as part of a Y2K car’s personality. “I don’t know what kind of disease that is in the brain,” says one TikTok creator, who has to pry open the fuel door of her 2003 Mitsubishi Outlander with a screwdriver . “But I don’t get frustrated. I’m like, ‘Oh, this is fun.’”
In a Y2K car that takes a lickin’ and keeps on tickin’, creature comforts are beside the point. For many, part of the appeal is the absence of dashboard infotainment displays and other screens that have replaced basic switches and knobs in newer cars, often in the name of cost-cutting. Automakers’ zeal to monetize in-car technology, sometimes charging extra to activate physically installed features such as heated seats and remote start, only reinforces young buyers’ doubts about the value of a new car.
At the same time, do-it-yourself repairs have become harder as cars grow more digitally complex and auto manufacturers cut off access to owners and even independent mechanics . Oftentimes, they require investing in specialty digital readers or computer software to diagnose problems, and bespoke tools for wrenching. Most car owners would sooner punt, take the car to the dealership and pay whatever the maintenance and repair costs – which, of course, is exactly the vertical integration that shareholder-bound manufacturers are after.
Hence the romance with Y2K cars: you can fix ‘em yourself, their old-school controls fall easily to hand, they’re tried and tested, seemingly built to last. They just have an aura of invincibility – never mind that their age makes them fundamentally more dangerous and susceptible to frequent repairs. “I’ve used my Jetta as if it were a truck,” Price says. “Transported trees in it, put my surfboard through the sunroof. I’ve done every single thing possible to thrash it beyond its abilities.”
Price’s passengers, however, don’t have much appreciation for Pewter Pebble’s quirks. Often while carpooling to US military installations, senior officers compelled to hold up the sagging headliner would ask him when he was trading in his beater for a new truck or SUV. It was a similar story when Price left the military last year and started chauffeuring Alex Vindman, the Iraq war veteran turned US Senate hopeful, on the campaign trail during Florida’s special election. “I drove him around a couple times in it, and he was like, ‘ What is going on?’” Price says. “The fact that we expect folks who are getting paid, like, a grand a month to have a new car is nuts.”
T wenty-five miles north-west of downtown Atlanta, a half hour’s drive in optimistic traffic, sits Town Center at Cobb, a typical suburban mall in recession. But on the first Sunday of every month, the mall parking comes alive for Caffeine and Octane, a sprawling car show that’s open to the public, free to attend and also has long lines for coffee and donut trucks. And even though the usual turnout of 2,000-plus cars was winnowed down to a few hundred on the gray, showery morning of October’s show, it was still an impressive array of vintage American muscle, Japanese domestic market (or JDM) unicorns and multimillion-dollar exotics. The Y2K cars stood out, too.
Sitting right at the entrance of the show was Anthony DeNaples’s 2000 Buick Regal GS, a sleeper sedan that has become a cult classic. He bought it four months ago for $18,000 on Facebook Marketplace, a price he considered a bargain for such a rare commuter. “Person didn’t really know what they had,” says the 37-year-old custom car builder, who uses the car to ferry his two young daughters. His oldest is constantly goading him to do burnouts, which she calls “making stripes”. Modern cars, he reasons, have become so laden with safety systems – for keeping the car in lane, or slamming on the brakes when sensors detect an obstacle – that they’re less fun to drive hard. “A lot of newer cars, if you want to drive it how it’s meant to be driven, y

articles.content_orig:
A proposed $34 billion merger between Johnson & Johnson’s orthopaedics business and Smith & Nephew would have involved approximately $10 billion in debt financing from the British medical-device maker while giving J&J shareholders 50.1% of the combined company, according to the Financial Times .
The financing component was more than three times Smith & Nephew’s $3.02 billion in net debt as of June 27, 2026.
Under the terms described by the outlet, the borrowing would have funded a roughly $10 billion payment to J&J, helping reconcile the businesses’ differing valuations. J&J’s orthopaedics operation was valued at up to $22 billion, compared with Smith & Nephew’s market capitalization of approximately $12.6 billion cited in the reporting.
Smith & Nephew’s latest published results show the financial scale involved. At the end of the first half, the company reported a net-debt-to-adjusted-EBITDA ratio of 1.8 times and free cash flow of $231 million, down from $244 million a year earlier.
In August, it maintained its full-year free cash flow forecast of approximately $800 million while reducing expected underlying revenue growth to around 4% from around 6%. The proposed $10 billion borrowing was equivalent to 12.5 times that standalone annual cash flow forecast, before accounting for earnings, borrowing costs, or other financial effects of a combined business.
Despite reported agreement on the transaction’s principal economics, the merger discussions broke down over management. The FT reported, citing people familiar with the negotiations, that J&J wanted DePuy Synthes president Namal Nawana to lead the combined company.
Smith & Nephew chairman Rupert Soames instead insisted that incumbent chief executive Deepak Nath retain the position, according to the report.
Nawana previously served as Smith & Nephew’s CEO, departing in 2019 amid a compensation disagreement. J&J had publicly designated Nawana as the expected leader of DePuy Synthes when it announced plans to separate the orthopaedics business in October 2025. The division generated $9.3 billion in sales in 2025, according to J&J’s financial results.
On October 13, J&J CEO Joaquin Duato said the company was leaning toward spinning off DePuy Synthes as a standalone company, with separation targeted for mid-2027.

articles.content_orig:
Investors ran for cover this week as artificial intelligence fears hit stocks, driving the 10-year Treasury below 5%.
The benchmark yield stayed below 5% on Friday, after falling beneath that level Thursday for the first time in a month, as investors continued to express misgivings over the massive debt being taken on by technology companies to finance their build out of AI networks. Tech stocks sank, bond yields on outstanding tech debt rose and spreads on credit default swaps widened in a host of AI companies.
"The selloff in tech stocks drove the flight-to-quality bid, compounded by continued weakness in the French sovereign market," BMO's credit strategy team said in a note Friday. "Interestingly, the focus on weakness in the equity market ... [has] overshadowed the move in the energy market, with Treasuries rallying despite WTI crude oil testing $100/bbl."
On Friday, yields on 10-year U.S. Treasurys — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose by 1 basis point to 4.966%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve policy, increased by 2 basis points to 4.658%. Yields on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasurys — which react to geopolitical developments — were relatively flat at 5.292%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The bounce back in Treasury prices comes just weeks after 10- and 30-year yields jumped to their highest levels in more than 20 years .
Since that time, concerns have grown about the billions being spent by tech companies. CoreWeave has led the rout, losing 10% on Thursday and 36% in October. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 stands at 15.72%, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is 1,138. Any reading above 1,000 is generally considered distressed.
Next week, the focus will turn to the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, due on Wednesday. The market doesn't expect the central bank to raise rates this month, but is pricing in a roughly 72% probability of a quarter percentage point hike in December, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool .
"At this stage, the tightening of financial conditions hasn't been dramatic enough to preclude another rate hike this year, although a sustained deterioration could readily alter the Fed's policy calculus," BMO Capital said.
Traders are awaiting Friday's flash S&P Global PMI readings on manufacturing and services for a fresh view on U.S. growth and inflation. Meanwhile, rising energy costs continue to weigh on the inflation outlook.
West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery climbed another 1.6% to $101.10 a barrel on Friday, while Brent crude , the international oil benchmark, traded 1.4% higher, at $114.71 a barrel.
Firmer energy prices come as fresh attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabian oil installations drove new fears over an oil supply squeeze. Reports earlier this week suggested that the U.S. and Israel could resume strikes against Iran following the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

articles.title_orig: How Congress could address Social Security insolvency – and the hidden cost
articles.title_zh: How Congress could address Social Security insolvency – and the hidden cost
articles.content_orig:
Kent Smetters, faculty director of the Penn Wharton Budget Model, on Social Security's looming funding crisis.
Social Security is expected to reach insolvency within a decade, and with the key safety net program facing the prospect of automatic benefit cuts when that occurs, a critical debate over the cost of replacing that revenue could be obscured by a budget rule.
Kent Smetters, faculty director of the Penn Wharton Budget Model, spoke exclusively with FOX Business about a new report that details how federal budget rules assume Social Security benefits would be paid in full using general revenue transfers when the program's trust funds reach insolvency in about six or seven years.
"What the law actually says is that when the trust fund depletes, benefits have to be reduced to a level that's consistent with just the monthly payroll taxes that come in. We estimate that to be about a 15% reduction of benefits, which is sizable," Smetters said, adding that the cut would apply to newcomers and existing enrollees alike.
FEDERAL BUDGET DEFICIT HITS $2T AS NATIONAL DEBT COSTS SURGE
Smetters said that a separate law covers how the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) would score the cost of trust fund depletion and general fund transfers to appear as if there was no cost to shifting borrowing to the general fund as spending continues.
Social Security benefits would be cut automatically by law if key trust funds reach insolvency, though a budget rule obscures the cost of transferring general revenue funds. (Al Drago/Getty Images)
"We all know that's just like the left hand paying the right hand or vice versa. It doesn't do anything to solve the actual funding problem. But nonetheless, that's going to score as though it's costless, zero dollars, even though that borrowing from general revenue will be substantial – almost 200% of GDP within 75 years, or over 400% of taxable payroll over 75 years," Smetters said.
He cautioned that the budget rule may "almost cast a die of what's going to actually happen, because I think policymakers are going to see that it's kind of like the easy button for looking like they've solved Social Security."
The approach of relying on general fund transfers to make up the shortfall to pay Social Security benefits in full could also raise alarm in bond markets and worsen the nation's fiscal woes through higher interest rates.
Smetters said that " bond markets are currently making a bet that Congress and the president will eventually get their act together, because if they don't, future bond markets are just going to pound them," adding that the general revenue transfers would serve as the "ultimate sign that we've given up."
AMERICA'S $40T NATIONAL DEBT IS 'STEALING FROM OUR NEXT GENERATION,' ECONOMIST WARNS
The CBO's most recent 10-year budget outlook estimated that Social Security's main trust fund would be depleted in 2032, with benefits reduced by an average of 28% annually after benefits are cut. The reduction in benefits would amount to about $2.7 trillion in reduced benefits over the 2032 to 2036 period, according to the CBO.
Smetters noted that while the CBO and Penn Wharton Budget Model projections differ slightly in the timing and extent of benefit cuts, as PWBM estimates insolvency will occur in 2033 with benefits reduced by 15%, policymakers need to address the fiscal challenges facing Social Security as soon as possible.
"Even though seven years is not that far away, the good news is there are a range of options," Smetters said, noting that the Penn Wharton Budget Model website has a set of seven illustrative options that range from heavy tax revenue increases to heavy benefit cuts, with a middle ground in between.
ONE TYPE OF SOCIAL SECURITY ADJUSTMENT COULD CUT THE 75-YEAR SHORTFALL IN HALF
Social Security is trending toward insolvency in 2032 or 2033, according to various projections. (Getty Images/stock)
Smetters said that while various solutions to prevent trust fund depletion and reduce federal debt have different long-term economic outcomes, there is still time for a rational discussion.
"Unless we go with the gimmick approach in terms of this general revenue transfer, the fact of the matter is it requires really having adults in the room on both sides of the aisle," he said.
Smetters highlighted the Social Security reforms made during the 1980s by then-President Ronald Reagan and Democratic House Speaker Tip O'Neill, which set partisanship aside.
"They decided we're jumping off this bridge together because the country is worth it, and they were going to put their personal politics, personal ambitions aside to solve this problem," Smetters said. "We just don't have that rhetoric right now."

articles.title_zh: Teen girl accused of helping Russia kill Ukrainian soldiers with poison
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian police said Friday they had detained a 17-year-old girl suspected of helping Russia's security services to poison Ukrainian soldiers and that two had died.
Ukraine and Russia have throughout their war since 2022 accused each other of recruiting minors for sabotage acts including poisoning.
The girl, who was not named, is suspected of having packaged deadly drugs and sending them to Ukrainian soldiers she contacted by Telegram,  police said in a statement.
She was arrested by police in Zhytomyr, west of Kyiv, after allegedly following instructions from a Russian handler in exchange for at least 5,000 hryvnias ($111), they said.
After receiving packages with "free drugs," the soldiers were "instructed to take them on camera," the statement said.
"The recipients did not know that the capsules contained a lethal dose of methadone," it said, adding that "two soldiers died from poisoning in the Zhytomyr region."
Police said they had identified other recipients of the packages, which "prevented four more murders" across the country.
"The young woman was notified that she is suspected of aiding and abetting the premeditated murder of two people as part of a prior conspiracy," the police statement said.
She was also suspected of "shipping drugs and psychotropic substances for the purpose of distribution," it said, adding that she faced up to 15 years in jail if found guilty.
Police cautioned that Russia aims "to kill our people and destabilize the situation within the country."
"Do not accept medication or other substances, as well as food or drinks of dubious origin, from people you do not know well," police cautioned.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukrainian authorities say they have opened thousands of investigations into collaboration with the enemy, and frequently arrest individuals accused of working for Moscow.
In 2023, Ukraine accused Russia of poisoning Marianna Budanova , the wife of Kyrylo Budanov, who was then head of Ukraine's military intelligence and is now a presidential adviser. Apart from Budanova, several personnel from Ukraine's military intelligence (known by its local acronym GUR) were also diagnosed with the same poisoning.
Also in 2023, Paris prosecutors opened an investigation into the suspected poisoning of a Russian journalist who made headlines when she brandished an anti-Ukraine war slogan on state television.
In an interview with the British tabloid The Sun, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that he's survived "no fewer" than five or six assassination attempts since Russia invaded Ukraine.

The incident has illustrated how AI is creating a new level of risk for businesses and consumers online, in a week when multiple other cyber threats caused headaches for security workers.
Here's what executives and analysts are saying about the biggest cyber threat of the moment — and how AI could make things even worse.
Anthropic's deputy security chief, Jason Clinton, warns that a "vulnerability tsunami" is coming — and says critical infrastructure hasn't caught up.
Clinton posted on X on Wednesday about the need to "patch critical infrastructure" before core network vulnerabilities get exploited. On Thursday, he issued another warning to companies.
"As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better," he wrote.
"Security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)," he added.
Andrew Curran, a prominent AI analyst, weighed in on several cybersecurity threats from Wednesday to Thursday.
"Regarding potential attacks on energy, food, and water infrastructure, the threat is quite real. Someone is currently probing infra and feeling it out, it is an active threat. Even a little preparation can be helpful, just in case," Curran wrote on Wednesday in response to an NSA cybersecurity advisory about threat actors.
On Thursday, Curran also highlighted a hack of Quest Diagnostics, which he said serves "roughly half" of the US's hospitals and physicians.
In February, Matt Shumer, the former CEO of Hyperwrite, published a viral essay on his website titled "Something Big Is Happening," in which he warned of large-scale disruptions wrought by AI that could upend the world order.
Shumer published another essay on Thursday on his website and LinkedIn, this time titled "The Internet Is Under Attack. Here's How to Protect Yourself and Your Family."
"Right now, as you read this, swarms of AI agents are likely trying to break into the websites you use. Not one of them. Many of them," Shumer wrote. "We are in the middle of the biggest cybersecurity moment in years."
This is what could happen, per Shumer's post:
Shumer also outlined four ways people can protect themselves, including updating all their software and staying off sites they're unfamiliar with while companies and websites alike make their security updates.
He also advises that people protect their bank accounts by being extra cautious about any and all codes and links that they receive. People should also "close the doors you aren't using" by unplugging smart gadgets and deleting apps that aren't being utilized.
"Every connected thing is another way in," Shumer wrote.
Marc Benioff agreed with Anthropic's Jason Clinton in an X post on Thursday.
"Jason is 100% right. Code red," Benioff wrote, along with a red alarm emoji.
Sriram Krishnan, a prominent venture capitalist and former senior AI policy advisor for President Donald Trump, said that the PHP vulnerabilities are a "harbinger of things to come" as AI models continue to detect long-standing cyber issues.
"However the entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes," he said in a post on X.
The new cyber reality may require more public-private partnerships to build the required infrastructure, he said.
The Menlo Venture partner Deedy Das warned that "the era of vibe hacking is here" in a series of posts on X.
He said he'd seen firsthand that "even non-technical people" can exploit common vulnerabilities, such as PHP, using AI models. Das said someone could theoretically direct certain models to any website and instruct them to quickly locate the vulnerabilities.
"Once you figure it out, it is downright trivial to do. The digital infrastructure of the world is at risk," he wrote.
AI agents have ended the era of "security through obscurity" because they can devote once-unthinkable time and effort to finding vulnerabilities, Box CEO Aaron Levie said on X. People will need to upgrade legacy infrastructure, modernize security policies, and tighten access controls, among other measures, he said.
"Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors," Levie wrote.
Yet Levie thinks humans also have an important role to play in the cyber revolution — he predicted a boom in cybersecurity jobs , which could become a huge investment area for companies.
"You will need more talent to point the agents at the most critical work, review findings, patch systems, respond to incidents, and more," he said.

articles.title_orig: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
articles.title_zh: Cyprus police open investigation into financial affairs of Roman Abramovich
articles.content_orig:
Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial affairs of Roman Abramovich, following revelations by BBC Panorama that accountancy firm Deloitte helped in falsifying documents to hide his wealth and evade tax.
Serious questions about the integrity of some of Abramovich's professional advisers were raised earlier this month in a joint report from the BBC and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ).
A Cypriot Ministry of Justice official told MPs this week that the report's findings would be looked at as part of a new investigation by the police's Financial Intelligence Unit.
Lawyers for Abramovich have said that he denies evading tax or concealing his fortune. Deloitte Cyprus said it acts "in compliance with applicable laws".
The police investigation was announced at a parliamentary committee meeting in the Cypriot capital, Nicosia, held to discuss the combating and prevention of money laundering.
The Ministry of Justice official told MPs the police would try to determine whether any criminal acts had been committed.
Last week, the report from the BBC and TBIJ detailed how accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus in 2006 meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts.
Deloitte, which is the world's largest accountancy firm, also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth, through the falsification of documents.
The evidence was contained in leaked files, including thousands of documents about Abramovich's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies, administered from Cyprus between 1995 and 2022.
The BBC and media partners including TBIJ, the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network, have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential investigation.
A representative from the Cypriot police, Andreas Anastasiades, confirmed to MPs that its Financial Crime Unit had already begun to gather evidence, and said the investigation was expected to last several months.
When asked by the BBC if the investigation would look into Deloitte's work, Andreas Anastasiades said: "We will look at any company or person who may be involved."
He added: "We will see if there has been fraud or if some documents have been manipulated."
Lawyers for Abramovich say that Panorama has provided no evidence that the billionaire knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document. They also say it was legitimate for his companies to rely on advice from professionals.
Deloitte Cyprus says it is unable to comment because the documents are more than 20 years old and no longer accessible.
The BBC and TBIJ have previously reported on a tax scheme that allowed Abramovich to dodge millions in tax on the running costs of his yachts.
Following that report, two former company directors have been indicted and are due to stand trial in Cyprus next month over €25m in unpaid VAT.
Mr Abramovich's lawyers previously told the BBC that he had "always obtained independent expert professional tax and legal advice" and "acted in accordance" with it.

articles.title_orig: ‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon towns
articles.title_zh: ‘This is a lethal threat’: Indigenous groups fear Bolsonaro’s hold on voters in Brazil’s Amazon towns
articles.content_orig:
Far-right presidential candidate is popular among those who believe more mining can help revitalise local economies
I t was the night before the first round of Brazil’s presidential election and Rosimari Monteiro was so excited she couldn’t sleep. The 38-year-old spent hours tossing and turning at her home in the Amazon town of Mucajaí before rising at dawn to cast her vote.
“I was the first person to vote at my polling station … I voted 22, so we got off to a positive start,” recalls Monteiro, as she stands in her sitting room with her two young daughters.
Twenty-two is the number Brazil’s electronic voting system uses to identify the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who is hoping to beat the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , in this year’s election.
“To us, he represents the future. We want a light at the end of the tunnel. We want a better future for ourselves and for our kids, who are the future of our nation,” enthuses Monteiro, who was far from the only person in Mucajaí to vote Bolsonaro.
In fact, this sun-baked roadside settlement is where Bolsonaro secured his biggest proportional victory in Roraima, the northern state where the would-be president also registered his best nationwide result . Nearly 79% of 11,734 votes in Mucajaí went to Bolsonaro.
Monteiro gave several reasons for her decision, including Bolsonaro’s pledges to fight crime and create jobs. But one issue explains why the son of the disgraced former president Jair Bolsonaro is so popular here and across Roraima, where 14 of 15 municipalities backed the far-right politician.
Mucajaí was the launchpad for much of the illegal gold rush in which tens of thousands of miners invaded the nearby Yanomami Indigenous territory during Jair Bolsonaro’s environmentally calamitous 2019-2022 presidency. Prospectors used the meandering Mucajaí River to sneak into those protected Indigenous lands near the border with Venezuela, bringing malaria, mercury poisoning, hunger and destruction to its 32,000 Indigenous people. Ranches carved out of Mucajaí’s rainforests conceal clandestine airstrips from which helicopters and planes ferried supplies, miners and sex workers into jungles that the Yanomami’s ancestors are thought to have occupied for at least 1,000 years.
When Lula beat Bolsonaro’s father in the 2022 election, the leftwinger launched a crackdown to evict those miners and cripple a multi-billion dollar illegal industry he blamed for a “genocide” against the Yanomami . A broader environmental offensive across the Amazon cut deforestation to its lowest levels since the late 80s.
Now, nearly four years later, Mucajaí’s electorate hopes a Bolsonaro victory in Sunday’s second round runoff will end that clampdown and allow the 21st century gold rush to resume. “The closure of the mines brought complete penury. It became really hard to find jobs,” complains Monteiro, a driving instructor whose brother-in-law worked in the mines.
Like many people in the area, Monteiro believes that, if elected, Bolsonaro will move to legalise mining on Indigenous lands “so people can get back to work”. Speaking in the Amazon on Tuesday, Bolsonaro vowed to be a president “who will turn the riches God has given us into riches for every single one of you”, adding: “Lula couldn’t give a shit about the Amazon.”
The prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency has caused panic among Indigenous leaders and conservationists – here in Roraima, and all over the Amazon. From January, when the new president takes power, at least seven of the nine Amazon states, including Roraima, will have pro-Bolsonaro governors. Congress will feature a record number of rightwing politicians hostile to Indigenous rights and environmental issues.
“By voting 22, Brazilians are signing a death certificate for the Yanomami, and Indigenous people in general,” says the Yanomami leader Júnior Hekurari, 40, who was on the frontline of efforts to protect his people during the humanitarian crisis that unfolded under Bolsonaro.
Already, Hekurari sees signs the miners are again preparing to flood Brazil’s biggest Indigenous territory. In the days after the 4 October first round, which Bolsonaro won by 47% to Lula’s 45.1% , Yanomami villagers reported receiving calls from illegal prospectors ordering them to clear remote runways so they could return.
Nilton Tubino, who has led Lula’s anti-mining crusade since 2023 , says “strange movements” have been detected on the outskirts of the territory, reinforcing suspicions miners are gearing up to pillage precious metals and tin ore used to make mobile phones .
Tubino, who calls Mucajaí the “nerve centre” of the illegal trade, believes Lula can recover from his first-round loss. “The election isn’t over until it’s over,” says Tubino.
But speaking at his group’s headquarters in Roraima’s capital, Boa Vista, Tubino admits his unit will close if Bolsonaro prevails. He fears environmental and Indigenous protection officials who have led Lula’s crackdown will be sidelined and persecuted, as happened under Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after the 2022 election. The consequences for the Yanomami will be dire.
“This is a lethal threat … to the very existence of these people, to their culture and cosmovision, and way of life,” Lula’s former environment minister, Marina Silva, has warned.
Gold mining is not the only reason Roraima’s voters back Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old evangelical Christian twice baptised in the Jordan River. The evangelical church’s rapid advance into the Amazon has also bolstered support, with prosperity theology striking a chord among those on Brazil’s fast-growing agricultural frontier.
Leandro Gentil, a political activist and pastor in Boa Vista, considers Bolsonaro a champion of the Christian values his church fights “tooth and nail” to defend. “Bolsonaro is practically a unanimity within our congregation … He’s the fresh oxygen we need to breathe,” Gentil adds, citing the politician’s opposition to same-sex marriage, abortion and drugs.
Similar views are heard in Mucajaí, where small evangelical temples are found on most streets.
Marinalva Ferreira Barbosa, a 40-year-old cleaner who worships at a local branch of the powerful Assemblies of God church, says she opposes Lula because he champions “things forbidden by the Bible”. “Like men getting with men, women with women – this kind of filth,” adds Barbosa, who works in the Paradise Pousada, a 15-room hotel that, because of the mining crackdown, is empty.
Bolsonaro’s hardline pledge to eliminate “narco-terrorists” – despite his own well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld – has also seduced voters in the Amazon, where organised crime groups are tightening their grip .
“Drugs could destroy our future,” says Bolsonaro activist Luciano Gomes, as he stares out across Mucajaí from a tourist view point. Several of the rundown streets below are scrawled with graffiti celebrating Brazil’s biggest criminal organisation, the PCC, or threatening to shoot rivals from the Red Command gang dead.
But Gomes’s main reason for supporting Bolsonaro is his desire for mining to be unleashed. “Our state has a wealth of mineral resources … gold, diamonds and rare earths that were discovered recently,” he says, insisting they can be exploited responsibly. “Bolsonaro champions the idea that miners aren’t crooks, they’re workers.”
On Sunday, Gomes will return to the polls to vote “22”, sporting a garish shirt emblazoned with images of the Bolsonaros and their ally, the US president, Donald Trump.
If Bolsonaro triumphs, Gomes will lead a procession of cars draped in Brazil and US flags 50 miles north to Boa Vista, to attend an all-night shindig in a square centred around the statue of a gold panner.
The most famous Yanomami leader, Davi Kopenawa, has other ideas. “I’m going to vote for my friend Lula … The Lula government is a friend of the native peoples,” says Kopenawa, 70, warning of conflict and resistanc

articles.title_zh: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
articles.content_orig:
The homepage of the PHP.net website is seen on October 22, 2026 in Singapore. Cyber-security flaws were recently identified in the popular PHP programming language, which is used on a vast number of websites across the world, including those of major companies and national governments. The PHP Foundation released two patches designed to fix the vulnerabilities. Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images hide caption
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."
This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.
Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.
OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."
Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.
The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.
"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.
As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.
Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.
In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."
Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.
Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.
"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "

Changing security norms and cash shortages push Japanese researchers to pursue state-funded defence tech projects
Japanese universities and other educational institutions more than doubled their applications for defence ministry research funding this year to a record 291, up from 123 last year, as Tokyo moves to strengthen its defence capabilities.
The increase is the clearest sign yet that academia’s decades-long resistance to military-linked work is diminishing.
The bids accounted for more than half the record 560 applications received by the ministry this year, up from 340 last year, with the rest coming from public research institutes and companies.
Of the 47 projects selected for funding under the 12.9 billion yen (US$82 million) programme, 30 will be led by university researchers, with 11 universities – including Osaka, Nagoya and Keio – winning grants for the first time.
